title: One month of building a real-time multiplayer game with AI agents: what worked and what didn't
author: Anotherstoryforu
selftext:
**What it is** *Mugunghwa* ("The Rose of Sharon has bloomed") is the Korean version of Red Light, Green Light, the playground game every Korean kid grows up with. You run while the tagger sings and freeze the moment they turn around. Move and you get hit with paint. It runs in the browser on phone or PC with up to 40 players per round, and bots fill empty spots. Since launch it's grown to 12 Korean stages plus a "world tour" with 3 maps in each of six countries (30 open maps in total), with a passport that collects a stamp per stage, an outfit shop and private rooms with join codes.

**Setup:** solo dev. Claude Code wrote most of the code, and Codex handled art assets and a second set of reviews. The two agents take turns on the same repo and leave each other a shared handoff note. The stack is Three.js on the client and one Cloudflare Durable Object per room on the server, both running the same simulation code.



# What AI made easy

**1. Speed to a playable version.** The first public version took about 3 days, from a single-player prototype on day 1 to online multiplayer on day 2. Sharing one simulation between client and server meant that practice mode, bots and the online room all run the same rules.

**2. Testing I would never have written by hand.** Every feature came with its own test script, and there are now a few dozen of them. I also had AI build a few tools:

* a headless screenshot tool, so I could check each stage visually after every change
* a bot simulator that plays hundreds of rounds per map and reports the clear rate

Today I eased a hard map from a 50% to a 56% bot clear rate by testing seven variants in a few minutes, instead of guessing.

**3. Stats that turn into fixes.** I asked for a stats page (clear rate per stage, why people get out, when they leave), and AI read it back to me. One example: on overseas maps, humans cleared 45–50% while bots cleared 57–73%, and about 73% of human outs were "stopped too late while running". The problem was human reaction time, not the map layout, so the fix was a small per-map reaction grace for humans plus a few layout changes.

**4. Content at a steady pace.** Each new country (3 maps, a new tagger character, an outfit and passport art) took about a day. Codex made the concept art and backgrounds and Claude Code built the maps and mechanics. Translation into 7 languages was done by AI too, but it hasn't been checked by native speakers yet.

# What AI didn't make easy

**1. The voice. This was the hardest part.** The whole game depends on the tagger's chant. It has to go fast and slow, cut off mid-sentence and fake you out. The AI voice generator gave me a raw sung line, but it took many rounds of work to make it right:

* I wrote down the melody every Korean kid knows (with Gemini's help) and pitch-corrected the voice syllable by syllable to match it
* I ran speech-to-text on every take to check that the words were still understandable
* I built 10 rhythm variations out of the result

Nothing about it was one click.

**2. Art tone drifts.** Generated assets often looked fine on their own but wrong in the game. A mascot pet came out "cute" in a way nobody could read, and I rejected it. A tomato-festival street looked like blood until we reworked it into crushed pulp. I redid the first Japan maps because their quality didn't match the rest. My rule now is to compare every asset against real in-game screenshots, never against other generated images.

**3. Cultural judgment is on you.** For the world tour, one early Japan map idea used a shrine approach path. It was a reasonable idea on paper, but it's a sensitive subject for Korean players, so I cut it. After that I wrote down rules for which landmarks a map can use and avoided branded or licensed things. AI won't make that call for you.

**4. Bots are not humans.** Bot clear rates are great for comparing two versions of a map, but they badly underestimate how hard a map feels to people. Real player data had to be the final judge.

**5. The agent can be confidently wrong about why something failed.** Several "failing" server tests turned out to be my test setup (wrong config flags per test), not the code. Now I ask for the cause to be proven before anything gets fixed.

Thank you for reading this long post.  
  
Although this was a rather rudimentary account of game development, I hope you found it helpful, and I’d appreciate it if you’d give the game below a try.



**Play (free, no sign-up):** [**https://mugunghwa.pages.dev/**](https://mugunghwa.pages.dev/)
